name: Blush white
lede: Blush white is a near-white with a faint pink cast, a 2010 xkcd survey name that pairs the family word [[blush]] with *white* rather than naming a new hue outright.

sections.title: Barely a color at all
sections.body: The xkcd survey files this as a family-word compound, built on the existing color [[blush]], and no other source in our library independently records the exact name [1][2]. Its origin beyond the 2010 survey entry is undocumented [2]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system's nearest block, pinkish white, is 3.1 units away, a close match that confirms the color is barely past true white [2]. In LCH it measures lightness 97, chroma just 4, hue 34 degrees, among the lowest-chroma colors in the library, closer to [[linen]] and [[ivory]] than to any strong pink [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our 23,781-painting archive, a color within six units of Blush white covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 55 paintings, about 0.23 percent of the archive, as photographed [3]. It most often plays a light, sitting among a painting's brightest areas in 86 percent of its appearances, which fits a near-white used for highlights and skin [3]. Its earliest match dates to the year 960, 1,050 years before the name was recorded in 2010; a faintly pink near-white is one of the easiest colors for an old varnished highlight to drift into, so this gap reflects the hue's ordinariness, not any connection to the modern name, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. In printed English the phrase peaked in the 1860s [4].

questions.q: Blush white is built as a compound of "white" and which other color name?
True or false: inside a painting, Blush white most often appears as one of the darker, shadowed areas.

openers: Blush white is barely a color: it measures only 4 points of chroma, next to nothing.

issues: No source beyond our own library's xkcd record; origin said plainly as undocumented.
